Abstract: The security of Large Language Models (LLMs) is a critical issue in their practical deployment. Current safety alignment relies primarily on fine-tuning to achieve human-aligned behavior. Similarly to software security issues, automated testing through fuzzing can be applied to LLMs to uncover potential vulnerabilities. Author Affiliations: Department of Artificial Intelligence, Chonnam National University, Gwangju, Republic of Korea; Department of Artificial Intelligence, Chonnam National University, Gwangju, Republic of Korea; Department of Artificial Intelligence, Chonnam National University, Gwangju, Republic of Korea; Department of Artificial Intelligence, Chonnam National University, Gwangju, Republic of Korea
Publication Title: IEEE Access
Abstract: Indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks have emerged as a critical security threat to large language model (LLM)-based email agents. However, existing evaluation benchmarks largely rely on simulated environments that cannot verify whether an attack will actually succeed in practice, often determining attack success solely based on tool invocation, which leads to frequent misclassifications of attack outcomes. In this paper, we propose execution-aware stage-wise evaluation (EASE) as an automated framework that quantitatively assesses the vulnerability of email agents to IPI attacks in a realistic environment integrated with the Gmail application programming interface (API) and multiple LLM APIs. EASE automates the entire pipeline of delivering attack emails, triggering the LLM agent, and collecting tool invocation logs, and judges attack success by whether the delivered email actually fulfills the attacker’s intent, using tool invocation only as a proxy baseline. Additionally, EASE’s modular architecture allows new LLMs, defense prompts, and attack datasets to be plugged in or replaced independently, and a Streamlit-based web interface makes the framework accessible to non-developers. To validate EASE’s effectiveness, we conducted 15,336 experiments using 639 attack samples across six LLMs under four defense conditions. The results demonstrate that executing attacks in the live service reveals what proxy-based judgment misses: 13.9% of proxy-judged successes are actually failures when the execution outcome is verified. We also observe that the same defense prompt can paradoxically increase the attack success rate for certain LLMs, underscoring the need for execution-grounded evaluation tools such as EASE. EASE is released as an open-source package on GitHub so that email agent developers and security researchers can adopt it immediately.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) models such as large language models (LLM) have demonstrated substantial advancements in recent years. Author Affiliations: Graduate School of Information, Production and Systems, Waseda University, Japan; Graduate School of Information, Production and Systems, Waseda University, Japan
Publication Title: 2025 IEEE 10th International Conference on Smart Cloud (SmartCloud)
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently gained popularity for tasks like text generation and automated reasoning, often hosted on cloud servers to handle large-scale user interactions. Yet this setup faces a critical challenge, prompt injection attacks, where adversaries craft malicious text to bypass an LLM’s safety constraints and policy filters. Attackers constantly evolve new injection tactics, rendering static defenses ineffective. While service providers may wish to store user inputs for security audits, this practice poses serious privacy and data-protection risks. User prompts can contain personal or confidential information subject to strict regulatory requirements. To address these conflicting demands of security monitoring and user privacy, we propose a privacy-preserving prompt injection detection scheme via hash and embedding-based auditing for smart cloud-deployed LLMs. Our approach segments each user prompt into smaller chunks and stores only non-invertible representations of them—cryptographic hashes for exact matches and vector embeddings for near-match detection. This enables robust identification of both verbatim and paraphrased threats without retaining any plaintext data. Furthermore, newly discovered injection patterns can trigger retrospective audits on previously stored chunks, greatly enhancing attack traceability. We also introduce an optional blockchain-based logging mechanism for tamper-proof event records. Empirical results show that our method achieves high detection accuracy against diverse injection techniques while safeguarding sensitive user information.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve remarkable advances in understanding and reasoning with human language, which are widely applied in software development, content creation, healthcare, etc. However, their vulnerabilities to security threats, especially jailbreak attacks, remain a significant issue. Existing research on jailbreak mainly focuses on the security risks of LLMs' inherent thinking and reasoning, overlooking the new attack surface introduced by web search capability. Attackers can exploit this by guiding LLMs to retrieve information from external URLs, which is then used to implicitly reconstruct harmful instructions and circumvent safety mechanisms, leading to the generation of harmful content. In this paper, we propose a novel jailbreak attack, named URLcoat. The core idea is to exploit the web search capabilities of LLMs to circumvent their security safeguards. URLcoat incorporates three core strategies: obfuscating the feature of sensitive words to evade input detection, reconstructing harmful instructions via implicit associations with external URLs, and contextual narrative guidance to bypass output filtering. This study examines the security vulnerabilities arising from lLMs' web search capability, which facilitates the LLMs to produce harmful output.

Publication Title: 2024 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)
Abstract: Few-shot classification with foundation models (e.g., CLIP, DINOv2, PaLM-2) enables users to build an accurate classifier with a few labeled training samples (called support samples) for a classification task. However, an attacker could perform data poisoning attacks by manipulating some support samples such that the classifier makes the attacker-desired, arbitrary prediction for a testing input. Empirical defenses cannot provide formal robustness guarantees, leading to a cat-and-mouse game between the attacker and defender. Existing certified defenses are designed for traditional supervised learning, resulting in sub-optimal performance when extended to few-shot classification. In our work, we propose FCert, the first certified defense against data poisoning attacks to few-shot classification. We show our FCert provably predicts the same label for a testing input under arbitrary data poisoning attacks when the total number of poisoned support samples is bounded. We perform extensive experiments on benchmark few-shot classification datasets with foundation models released by OpenAI, Meta, and Google in both vision and text domains. Our experimental results show our FCert: 1) maintains classification accuracy without attacks, 2) outperforms existing state-of-the-art certified defenses for data poisoning attacks, and 3) is efficient and general.

Abstract:
Summary

This chapter exposes one of the most insidious threats in modern artificial intelligence (AI) systems: adversarial fine‐tuning and model reprogramming. It explores how attackers exploit standard fine‐tuning processes to subtly alter generative model behavior, embedding malicious, biased, or unauthorized outputs that activate only under specific conditions. Through targeted manipulation of training data, gradient updates, and prompt structures, adversaries can reshape the logic of a model without affecting its performance on traditional benchmarks—making detection both difficult and critical.

Readers will gain a clear understanding of how semantic perturbations, prompt conditioning, and gradient‐aligned Trojans allow covert behaviors to be embedded deep within transformer models. The chapter outlines how adversaries test and optimize these behaviors for persistence, stealth, and cross‐model transferability, even across different architectures and deployment contexts. These techniques are not fringe cases—they represent a growing class of scalable, low‐cost threats that bypass traditional security assumptions.

The chapter also equips readers with a defender's mindset, offering strategic guidance for identifying behavioral drift, verifying model provenance, and stress‐testing prompt responses. By framing reprogramming as a lifecycle risk—rather than an isolated event—it reinforces the need for continuous validation across the model development pipeline. This is essential reading for AI security professionals, risk managers, and engineers tasked with deploying safe and trustworthy generative systems in real‐world environments.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures have become a prevalent paradigm for scaling large language models, yet their sparse routing mechanisms introduce unique security risks: safety alignment tends to concentrate in a small subset of experts, creating a structural vulnerability. Existing backdoor methods against MoE models typically follow a data-driven paradigm, embedding malicious logic in model weights through data poisoning and fine-tuning, which leaves them susceptible to weight-based defenses. In this paper, we introduce an architectural backdoor that hard-codes detection and intervention logic directly into the model's computation graph, decoupling the backdoor from model weights. We design a handcrafted arithmetic punctuation trigger that can be injected without altering semantic content and detected via mathematical methods. Upon trigger detection, we intervene in the routing process by suppressing pre-identified safety experts, redirecting tokens toward non-safety experts to enable jailbreak outputs. We evaluate our method on seven mainstream MoE models across three safety benchmarks. Experimental results show that our approach achieves up to 96.0% jailbreak success rate with improvements of up to 47 percentage points over the baseline. The backdoor persists under full-model fine-tuning, outperforming the data-driven BadSwitch method by up to 65 percentage points under identical conditions. Ablation studies further validate that precise safety-expert localization is essential for effectiveness. Our work highlights a supplychain security risk in MoE architectures, where architecturallevel computation graph modifications can introduce persistent backdoors that evade conventional defenses.

It emphasizes the importance of understanding internal model structures, context‐aware manipulation techniques, and adversarial testing that mirrors how attackers condition models across time, input structure, and retrieved data. With clear analysis and applied framing, this chapter equips readers to identify, evaluate, and begin defending against the behavioral exploits that define modern generative AI threats.

Abstract: Tool-integrated large language model (LLM) agents can call files, databases, email systems, web search, and code execution tools, which turns tool use into a runtime authorization problem. Sandboxed live planning traces from gpt-5.4, gemini-3.1-propreview, deepseek-v4-flash, and kimi-k2.6 further test interception at the model-tool boundary. Claims remain limited to controlled benchmarks and sandboxed traces. The main innovation is an intent-bound behavior-chain authorization event enforced before executor access. The evaluation covers controlled guardrail baselines, per-call authorization latency, adversarial prompt robustness, and structural multi-agent scalability under controlled and sandboxed settings.

Abstract: Sources of overfitting in deep neural net (DNN) classifiers include: 1) large class imbalances; 2) insufficient training set diversity; and 3) over-training. Whereas backdoor mitigation and other adversarial learning defenses often trade off a classifier’s accuracy to achieve robustness against attacks, our approach, inspired by ideas from adversarial learning, helps the classifier’s generalization accuracy: as shown for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, our approach improves both the accuracy for rare categories as well as overall. Abstract:
Summary

As artificial intelligence (AI) systems move from research labs into production environments, they introduce fundamentally different architectures and operational behaviors that redefine what it means to secure software. This chapter explores the structural distinctions between predictive, generative, and agentic AI, explaining how their internal mechanisms shape risk exposure, attack surfaces, and defensive priorities. From supervised models optimized for speed and accuracy to large language models capable of generating text and executing tools, each architecture comes with unique adversarial challenges—ranging from input manipulation to autonomous decision hijacking.

The chapter also walks through the AI development lifecycle, from data ingestion to post‐deployment monitoring, revealing how vulnerabilities can be introduced at each phase. It emphasizes the importance of recognizing adversarial entry points—not just in APIs or user prompts, but in training data, model fine‐tuning, and third‐party integrations. Readers gain practical insight into how attacks like model poisoning, prompt injection, and supply chain compromise exploit architectural and process‐level blind spots.

Crucially, this chapter introduces the concept of security debt—accumulated risk resulting from rushed development, lack of robustness testing, or weak observability. It shows how ignoring security early in the lifecycle compounds risk downstream, often surfacing only during high‐stakes deployment. By combining architectural literacy with lifecycle threat awareness, this chapter equips cybersecurity professionals to proactively assess and defend AI systems before adversaries do.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is an emerging approach in natural language processing that combines large language models (LLMs) with external document retrieval to produce more accurate and grounded responses. Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed to operate industrial systems through structured tool calls to Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) and Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems interfaces. Despite recent progress in agent safety, standardized benchmarks for evaluating step-level tool-call safety in industrial environments remain lacking. In this work, we present a guardrail-oriented dataset and benchmark for industrial LLM agents. We propose a three-mode safety taxonomy that distinguishes benign, injected-benign, and malicious requests, capturing both explicit attacks and covert contextual manipulations that induce unsafe behaviors in otherwise legitimate tasks. We further design a challenging cross-domain benchmark spanning six industrial domains, including water treatment, semiconductor manufacturing, pharmaceutical fermentation, oil refining, nuclear cooling, and food processing. The benchmark enforces domain-specific entity naming, realistic numeric values, and constraint mismatches where physical safety limits are stricter than PLC register bounds, enabling systematic evaluation of guardrail generalization under distribution shift. Experimental results show that strong instruction-tuned LLMs, while effective at handling explicitly malicious requests, struggle to detect unsafe behaviors induced by contextual prompt injection, revealing a critical blind spot in existing safety mechanisms. In contrast, a guardrail model fine-tuned on our dataset demonstrates substantially improved sensitivity to step-level safety violations, particularly in injected-benign scenarios, while maintaining robust performance against explicit attacks. These findings highlight the necessity of step-level supervision and the effectiveness of the proposed benchmark for developing reliable industrial agent guardrails. Our dataset and benchmark provide a standardized testbed for step-level tool-call safety in industrial LLM agents and establish a foundation for future research on safe and reliable autonomous industrial systems.

Author Affiliations: Software Engineering for AI Team CSIRO, Data61, Sydney, NSW, Australia; Data61, CSIRO, Sydney, NSW, Australia; Data61, CSIRO, Sydney, NSW, Australia; Software and Computational Systems (SCS) Research Program, Data61, CSIRO, Sydney, NSW, Australia; Data61, CSIRO, Sydney, NSW, Australia
Publication Title: IEEE Software
Abstract: Large Language Models and agents are deployed across domains, yet AI safety evaluations remain largely English-centric and model-focused. Because many LLMs are predominantly trained on English, minority-language prompts may expose vulnerabilities, which can be amplified when models operate as agents. To address this gap, members of the International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science across nine countries launched multilingual AI safety evaluations initiated by Singapore. In Australia, the Department of Industry, Science and Resources led national participation, coordinating technical experts including CSIRO’s Data61. Data61 conducted Mandarin Chinese testing across two evaluations, covering both model-level and agent-level safety. In total, we evaluated 699 prompt-injection requests and 156 agentic tasks. Results show weaker safeguards and higher evaluator disagreement in Mandarin compared to English, with risks further amplified in agentic settings. These findings underscore the need to distinguish model robustness from system-level safety and to strengthen multilingual AI safety evaluation.

Document Title: Reasoning Introduces New Poisoning Attacks Yet Makes Them More Complicated
Authors: H. Foerster; I. Shumailov; Y. Zhao; H. Chaudhari; J. Hayes; R. Mullins; Y. Gal
Author Affiliations: University of Cambridge; Google DeepMind; Imperial College London; Northeastern University; Google DeepMind; University of Cambridge; University of Oxford
Publication Title: 2026 IEEE Conference on Secure and Trustworthy Machine Learning (SaTML)
Abstract: Early research into data poisoning attacks against Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrated the ease with which backdoors could be injected. More recent LLMs add step-by-step reasoning, expanding the attack surface to include the intermediate chain-of-thought (CoT) and its inherent trait of decomposing problems into subproblems. Using these vectors for more stealthy poisoning, we introduce "decomposed reasoning poison", in which the attacker modifies only the reasoning path, leaving prompts and final answers clean, and splits the trigger across multiple, individually harmless components. Fascinatingly, while it remains possible to inject these decomposed poisons, reliably activating them to change final answers (rather than just the CoT) is surprisingly difficult. This difficulty arises because the models can often recover from backdoors that are activated within their thought processes. Ultimately, it appears that an emergent form of backdoor robustness is originating from the reasoning capabilities of these advanced LLMs, as well as from the architectural separation between reasoning and final answer.

Authors: E. A. de Amorim; C. Zanchettin
Author Affiliations: TELUS Digital Research Hub, CIAAM-USP, São Paulo, SP, Brazil; Centro de Informática, Universidade Federal de Pernambuco, Recife, PE, Brazil
Publication Title: 2026 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN)
Abstract: Language Models (LMs) are vulnerable to jailbreak prompts designed to bypass safety constraints. Despite the growing literature in English, resources and defenses tailored to the Portuguese language remain scarce. We present SecBERT, a specialized Portuguese classifier built on the BERTimbau Base architecture to detect policy-violating and harmful prompts. We construct a 29,432-instance Portuguese dataset by translating a subset of WildJailbreak, explicitly preserving the original four-way taxonomy (Vanilla/Adversarial vs. Benign/Harmful) to enable granular analysis. We evaluate multiple BERT-based backbones in both frozen and fine-tuned settings, using F1-score, AUC, and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) statistic to characterize operational separability. The fine-tuned BERTimbau Base (SecBERT) achieves 95.6% F1, 99.2% AUC, and 91.2% KS, significantly outperforming non-Portuguese-centric baselines in discriminatory capability. We further analyze threshold behavior and discuss the limitations of translation-based data generation, outlining directions for native Portuguese harmful prompt datasets and adaptive robustness testing.

Document Title: Authenticated and Offline-Verifiable Agent-to-Agent Messaging for LLM Agents
Authors: A. Alshammari; S. Assiri; H. Bahsi
Author Affiliations: School of Informatics and Computing, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, Arizona, USA; College of Engineering and Computer Science Jazan University, Jazan, Saudi Arabia; School of Informatics and Computing, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, Arizona, USA
Publication Title: 2026 IEEE 16th Annual Computing and Communication Workshop and Conference (CCWC)
Abstract: The latest A2A systems often use LLM-based agents for tool calling and planning workflows, introducing risks such as prompt injection attacks. We introduce a lightweight, proof-carrying receipt for agent-to-agent (A2A) messaging that supports fully offline verification. This receipt enables third parties to verify who authored a message and confirm whether it was logged, without contacting the sender, the receiver, or any online service. An agent signs a canonical JSON representation of each message. Servers log the payload hash in a Merkle tree and periodically sign the tree state as a Signed Tree Head (STH). The returned bundle includes a receipt containing a Merkle proof, an STH, and a minimal decentralized identifier (DID) registry for offline key discovery. A verifier recomputes the Merkle root and validates the payload-hash match, Merkle inclusion, and both the STH and client signatures entirely offline. In our prototype, the proof size grows as $O(\log N)$, and the median offline verification time is approximately 0.4 s on our test platform. Receipts self-authenticate individual messages within a single transparency log, providing a lightweight alternative to other approaches.

Publication Title: 2026 International Conference on Cybersecurity and AI-Based Systems (Cyber-AI)
Abstract: Agentic AI (Artificial Intelligence) systems introduce a new class of security risks because they combine large model reasoning with autonomy, memory, planning, tool use, environmental interaction, and, in some cases, multi-agent coordination. These capabilities create various opportunities for adaptive automation and decision support, and they further expand the attack surface beyond conventional model-centric AI security by enabling cascading actions, privilege misuse, adversarial prompt manipulation, memory poisoning, tool-chain compromise, and unsafe behavior under uncertainty. Along these lines, this research addresses the need for formal security risk assessment methods for Agentic AI systems by proposing a modelling framework that integrates static threat, vulnerability, and impact estimation, causal reachability analysis, time varying vulnerability modelling, agent-level expected loss, and threshold-based human override. To demonstrate its applicability, the framework is instantiated in a simulation of an LLM-based autonomous military decision-making system operating under stochastic policy behavior, adversarial jailbreak risk, and command defined risk thresholds. The results show that risk aware filtering can substantially reduce unsafe autonomous actions, increase safe human deferral, and preserve mission success under adversarial and epistemic uncertainty. Through this effort, this study contributes to the development of safer, more transparent, and more accountable autonomous decision-making architectures.

Abstract: The rapid deployment of generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) systems has introduced a new class of technical privacy risks that exceed the scope of traditional data protection frameworks. This paper investigates these emerging vulnerabilities through the lens of the OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Models (LLMs) - 2025 edition, correlating them with real-world privacy failures from $2023-2025$. It categorizes incidents such as prompt injection, model poisoning, excessive agency, and improper output handling, drawing connections between architectural design choices and user-level data exposure. High-profile cases - including OpenAI's GDPR fine by Italy's Garante, the Hugging Face transformer compromise, and the Reddit-Anthropic dispute illustrate the systemic nature of GenAI risks. In parallel, the study evaluates international regulatory and governance responses, including the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, and China's algorithmic controls, highlighting their strengths and implementation gaps. The analysis reveals that technical vulnerabilities often cascade across the GenAI lifecycle, creating enforcement blind spots and compliance challenges. The paper concludes by advocating for a holistic, cross-functional risk management strategy that integrates secure-by-design principles, real-time oversight, and proactive alignment with evolving regulatory standards.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence is reshaping how we understand and act on cyber threats. By learning from data, spotting hidden patterns, and sifting through vast amounts of information it helps us catch attacks faster and more accurately. This study systematically reviews 15 peer-reviewed studies to see exactly how these technologies, such as machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and knowledge graphs, fit into modern threat intelligence. The studies indicate that AI-powered tools can boost detection accuracy to nearly 95% while cutting out almost 40% of false alarms. Automated response platforms such as Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) can reduce the time it takes to address an incident by over half. Despite these advancements, these systems remain vulnerable to different cyber-attacks such as adversarial attacks, data poisoning, and systemic biases. The studies show that cyber-attacks can bypass AI detection with a 43% success rate, while poisoning datasets can degrade the model's performance by 22%. Moreover, biases in AI models result in undermining trust and reliability in global threat intelligence. Tackling these challenges requires more advanced AI models, like Explainable AI (XAI) techniques for transparency, Quantum AI to improve processing speed, and hybrid AI models that combine machine learning with knowledge-based reasoning. Introducing AI into cybersecurity workflows offers the potential to revolutionize this field. However, it should be handled with caution due to the complexity of the models. The priority on developing more resilient models to mitigate bias and keep these solutions scalable and interpretable is what future research focuses on. The emergence of knowledge graphs, large language models, and their effectiveness will depend on overcoming these challenges. ensuring that the CTI solutions are precise and trustworthy.
